flow.title: Flow: An Experimental Focus + Relaxation Index
flow.seoTitle: Flow: An Experimental Focus + Relaxation Index

sections.heading: What this number is
sections.body: Flow here is an experimental index that tries to capture a combination people often describe during absorbed work: attention that holds steady while the body stays reasonably calm. The browser tool cannot read your attention or your mind. It only combines two of its other indices, Focus and Relaxation, which themselves come from your heart rate and the irregularity of your beat-to-beat intervals.

sections.heading: How this tool calculates it
sections.body: Flow = 0.6 × Focus + 0.4 × Relaxation, limited to 0–100%. The tool works on a rolling 15-second window of fingertip video (about 30 frames per second), finds each pulse peak, keeps only beat-to-beat (RR) intervals between 400 and 1,500 ms that are within 22% of the median, and smooths the displayed numbers so they change gradually. Because Focus and Relaxation both rise when your heart rate is moderate and your rhythm is steady (low CSI), Flow rises in the same situations.

bullets.label: Higher
bullets.text: Your pulse was moderate and your beat intervals were fairly even during the reading. That can accompany calm, engaged attention, but it can also simply mean you sat still with a clean signal.

bullets.label: Lower
bullets.text: Heart rate was higher, the rhythm looked more irregular, or both. Movement, finger pressure changes and poor lighting push it down too, because they add noise to the camera signal.

sections.heading: Important limits
sections.body: This is an experimental heuristic built from a few camera-derived inputs. It is not a validated physiological measure, it is not emotion detection, and it is not a medical test. Treat it as a rough hint about the direction your signal is moving, not as a verdict about how you feel. The psychological state called "flow" is studied with questionnaires and task performance, and there is no accepted way to detect it from a 15-second fingertip reading.

bullets.label: Reduce interruptions
bullets.text: Close notifications and pick one task. Frequent switching is a reliable way to break concentration.

bullets.label: Slow breathing before deep work
bullets.text: A few minutes of slow, relaxed breathing often lowers heart rate a little and makes the rhythm steadier.

bullets.label: Sleep and breaks
bullets.text: Attention is easier to sustain when you are rested; short breaks every hour or so help too.

sections.body: The ONDA app is a separate product: it focuses on pulse, breathing and, with an Apple Watch, coherence. It does not use the formulas on this page.

sections.highlight: Use Flow as a curiosity, not a score to chase: it goes up when your pulse is moderate and your rhythm is steady.

sections.heading: What this number is
sections.body: Fatigue on this page is an experimental index. It is not a measure of sleepiness, muscle fatigue or overtraining. It is computed from two other indices in the tool, Energy and Stress, so it rises when your heart rate is above about 75 bpm and when your beat-to-beat rhythm looks irregular.

sections.heading: How this tool calculates it
sections.body: Fatigue = 60 × (1 − Energy/100) + 0.2 × Stress, limited to 0–100%. Energy falls as heart rate climbs above 75 bpm and as CSI (the irregularity of your beat intervals) rises; Stress is CSI × 130. The tool works on a rolling 15-second window of fingertip video (about 30 frames per second), finds each pulse peak, keeps only beat-to-beat (RR) intervals between 400 and 1,500 ms that are within 22% of the median, and smooths the displayed numbers so they change gradually.

bullets.label: Higher
bullets.text: Your pulse was elevated and/or your beat intervals varied a lot relative to their average. Being tired can do this, but so can coffee, having just climbed stairs, talking, or a noisy camera signal.

bullets.label: Lower
bullets.text: Heart rate was moderate and the rhythm looked steady during the reading.

sections.heading: Important limits
sections.body: This is an experimental heuristic built from a few camera-derived inputs. It is not a validated physiological measure, it is not emotion detection, and it is not a medical test. Treat it as a rough hint about the direction your signal is moving, not as a verdict about how you feel. Real fatigue assessment usually looks at trends over days (resting heart rate, HRV measured the same way each morning, sleep), not a single short reading.

bullets.label: Consistent sleep
bullets.text: Regular bed and wake times are one of the most dependable ways to feel less worn out.

bullets.label: Track trends, not moments
bullets.text: If you want to monitor recovery, measure at the same time each day, sitting still, and look at the week rather than one number.

bullets.label: Easy movement and breaks
bullets.text: A short walk or a few minutes of slow breathing can help you reset during a long day.

sections.body: The ONDA app is a separate product: it focuses on pulse, breathing and, with an Apple Watch, coherence. It does not use the formulas on this page.

sections.highlight: A high Fatigue value is a prompt to check the basics (sleep, caffeine, recent activity), not a diagnosis.

sections.heading: What this number is
sections.body: Excitement here is an experimental index of general physiological arousal. It rises with heart rate above 60 bpm and, a little, with breathing rate. It cannot tell positive excitement apart from nervousness, physical effort or caffeine, because the body shows all of these with a faster pulse.

sections.heading: How this tool calculates it
sections.body: Excitement = 1.5 × (heart rate − 60) + 0.5 × breathing rate, limited to 0–100%. Heart rate is 60,000 divided by the average RR interval; breathing rate is estimated from slow changes in the pulse signal and counts as 0 when the tool cannot find a clear rhythm. The tool works on a rolling 15-second window of fingertip video (about 30 frames per second), finds each pulse peak, keeps only beat-to-beat (RR) intervals between 400 and 1,500 ms that are within 22% of the median, and smooths the displayed numbers so they change gradually.

bullets.label: Higher
bullets.text: Your heart rate was well above 60 bpm. At 80 bpm and 15 breaths per minute, for example, the index is about 38%; at 100 bpm it is about 68%.

bullets.label: Lower
bullets.text: Your pulse was close to 60 bpm or below. Many relaxed, fit adults sit here at rest.

sections.heading: Important limits
sections.body: This is an experimental heuristic built from a few camera-derived inputs. It is not a validated physiological measure, it is not emotion detection, and it is not a medical test. Treat it as a rough hint about the direction your signal is moving, not as a verdict about how you feel. In practice this index is mostly a rescaled heart rate, so it carries the same caveats as heart rate itself.

bullets.label: Name the cause
bullets.text: If the number is high, ask what just happened: movement, coffee, a stressful message, or anticipation. The body response is similar in each case.

bullets.label: Slow exhale to settle
bullets.text: If you want to calm down, a few breaths with a longer exhale than inhale tend to lower heart rate over a minute or two.

sections.body: The ONDA app is a separate product: it focuses on pulse, breathing and, with an Apple Watch, coherence. It does not use the formulas on this page.

sections.highlight: Excitement is essentially "how far above 60 bpm is your pulse right now", expressed as a percentage.

sections.heading: What this number is
sections.body: Focus here is an experimental index. It does not measure attention, and a camera on your fingertip cannot know what you are thinking about. It averages two other indices in the tool, Energy and inverse Stress, so it is highest when your heart rate is moderate (at or below about 75 bpm) and your beat-to-beat rhythm is steady.

sections.heading: How this tool calculates it
sections.body: Focus = 0.5 × Energy + 0.5 × (100 − Stress), limited to 0–100%. Energy = 90 − 1.5 × (heart rate above 75 bpm) − 80 × CSI; Stress = 130 × CSI, where CSI is the standard deviation of your RR intervals divided by their mean. The tool works on a rolling 15-second window of fingertip video (about 30 frames per second), finds each pulse peak, keeps only beat-to-beat (RR) intervals between 400 and 1,500 ms that are within 22% of the median, and smooths the displayed numbers so they change gradually.

bullets.label: Higher
bullets.text: Moderate pulse and even beat intervals during the reading. This can go along with calm, steady work, but a relaxed person reading nothing at all will score the same.

bullets.label: Lower
bullets.text: A faster pulse, a more irregular rhythm, or a noisy signal from finger movement.

sections.heading: Important limits
sections.body: This is an experimental heuristic built from a few camera-derived inputs. It is not a validated physiological measure, it is not emotion detection, and it is not a medical test. Treat it as a rough hint about the direction your signal is moving, not as a verdict about how you feel. Heart signals change with concentration in lab studies, but not in a way that lets a short camera reading tell you how focused you are.

bullets.label: One task at a time
bullets.text: Set a clear goal for the next 25–50 minutes and remove obvious distractions.

bullets.label: Calm body first
bullets.text: Slow breathing for a few minutes before demanding work can lower arousal if you feel wired.

bullets.label: Rest
bullets.text: Sleep, hydration and regular breaks do more for concentration than any single number.

sections.body: The ONDA app is a separate product: it focuses on pulse, breathing and, with an Apple Watch, coherence. It does not use the formulas on this page.

sections.highlight: Focus rises when your pulse is moderate and your rhythm is steady. It is a hint about your body, not a reading of your mind.

sections.heading: What this number is
sections.body: Relaxation here is an experimental index that goes up when your beat-to-beat rhythm looks steady and your Energy index is high (which in this tool mostly means your heart rate is not above about 75 bpm). It is not a measure of how calm you feel, and it is not a validated relaxation score.

sections.heading: How this tool calculates it
sections.body: Relaxation = 60 × (1 − min(1, 1.5 × CSI)) + 0.2 × Energy, limited to 0–100%. CSI is the standard deviation of your RR intervals divided by their mean. Note that breathing rate is not part of this formula, even though slow breathing often does help you relax. The tool works on a rolling 15-second window of fingertip video (about 30 frames per second), finds each pulse peak, keeps only beat-to-beat (RR) intervals between 400 and 1,500 ms that are within 22% of the median, and smooths the displayed numbers so they change gradually.

bullets.label: Higher
bullets.text: Your RR intervals varied little relative to their average, and your pulse was moderate. Sitting still with a clean signal pushes it up.

bullets.label: Lower
bullets.text: The rhythm looked more irregular (higher CSI) or your pulse was faster. Finger movement also adds irregularity and lowers the score.

sections.heading: Important limits
sections.body: This is an experimental heuristic built from a few camera-derived inputs. It is not a validated physiological measure, it is not emotion detection, and it is not a medical test. Treat it as a rough hint about the direction your signal is moving, not as a verdict about how you feel. One quirk: in real physiology, a relaxed body often shows more beat-to-beat variation linked to breathing, while this index rewards less variation. That is one more reason to treat it as a rough hint only.

bullets.label: Slow breathing
bullets.text: Breathing slowly, around 5.5–6 breaths per minute (individually about 4.5–7) with a relaxed longer exhale, is a well-studied way to calm the body for most people.

bullets.label: Posture and stillness
bullets.text: Sit comfortably, drop your shoulders and rest your hand so the finger stays on the lens without pressing hard.

bullets.label: A few quiet minutes
bullets.text: Heart rate usually settles over several minutes of rest, not seconds.

sections.body: The ONDA app is a separate product: it focuses on pulse, breathing and, with an Apple Watch, coherence. It does not use the formulas on this page.

sections.highlight: Relaxation here mostly reflects a moderate pulse and a steady-looking rhythm. How you feel matters more than the number.

sections.heading: What this number is
sections.body: Alarm here is an experimental index built from rhythm irregularity and breathing rate. It is not an anxiety test and it cannot detect fear or worry. It rises when your beat-to-beat intervals look irregular relative to their average (high CSI) and when your estimated breathing rate is above 15 breaths per minute.

sections.heading: How this tool calculates it
sections.body: Alarm = 0.7 × Stress + 3 × (breathing rate − 15, if above 15), limited to 0–100%. Stress = 130 × CSI. Heart rate itself is not part of this formula. Breathing rate is estimated from slow swings in the pulse signal and counts as 0 when no clear rhythm is found. The tool works on a rolling 15-second window of fingertip video (about 30 frames per second), finds each pulse peak, keeps only beat-to-beat (RR) intervals between 400 and 1,500 ms that are within 22% of the median, and smooths the displayed numbers so they change gradually.

bullets.label: Higher
bullets.text: Beat intervals varied a lot relative to their mean and/or breathing was estimated above 15 per minute. Talking, moving your finger, cold fingers or dim light can raise it as much as a stressful moment can.

bullets.label: Lower
bullets.text: The rhythm looked steady and breathing was estimated at 15 per minute or slower.

sections.heading: Important limits
sections.body: This is an experimental heuristic built from a few camera-derived inputs. It is not a validated physiological measure, it is not emotion detection, and it is not a medical test. Treat it as a rough hint about the direction your signal is moving, not as a verdict about how you feel. If you feel anxious or unwell, trust that feeling over this number and seek appropriate help. A low score does not mean you are fine, and a high score does not mean something is wrong.

bullets.label: Longer exhales
bullets.text: Breathing in for about 4 seconds and out for about 6 is a simple way to slow down when you feel keyed up.

bullets.label: Re-measure calmly
bullets.text: Sit, rest your arm on a table, keep your finger still, and measure again after a minute. Many high readings are signal noise.

bullets.label: Physiological sigh
bullets.text: Two short inhales through the nose followed by a long exhale is another quick, low-effort way to settle.

sections.body: The ONDA app is a separate product: it focuses on pulse, breathing and, with an Apple Watch, coherence. It does not use the formulas on this page.

sections.highlight: Alarm reacts to an irregular-looking rhythm and faster breathing. Check the signal and your surroundings before reading anything into it.

sections.heading: What this number shows
sections.body: HR Acceleration here is a small number that describes whether your beat-to-beat intervals were, on average, getting longer or shorter from one beat to the next during the last 15 seconds. Despite its name, it is a simple average of successive differences, not a true second derivative of heart rate.

sections.heading: How this tool calculates it
sections.body: The tool takes the differences between consecutive RR intervals (in ms), averages them (skipping the first one), and divides by 100. The tool works on a rolling 15-second window of fingertip video (about 30 frames per second), finds each pulse peak, keeps only beat-to-beat (RR) intervals between 400 and 1,500 ms that are within 22% of the median, and smooths the displayed numbers so they change gradually.

bullets.label: Positive
bullets.text: RR intervals were getting longer on average, which means heart rate was drifting down during the window. This often happens during a slow exhale or as you settle.

bullets.label: Negative
bullets.text: RR intervals were getting shorter, so heart rate was drifting up, for example on an inhale, after moving, or as you get tense.

bullets.label: Near zero
bullets.text: No clear drift. This is the most common value at rest, because the natural speed-up and slow-down with each breath cancels out.

sections.heading: Why it jumps around
sections.body: Your heart naturally speeds up a little when you breathe in and slows when you breathe out (respiratory sinus arrhythmia). Over a 15-second window that contains only two or three breaths, where the window starts and ends in the breathing cycle strongly affects this value. Camera timing errors of a few milliseconds per beat add more noise. Small values in either direction are best read as "no meaningful change".

sections.heading: Important limits
sections.body: This is not a standard clinical or sports-science metric, and there are no established normal ranges for it. It is shown as a quick directional indicator only, not as a medical or fitness measurement.
The ONDA app is a separate product: it focuses on pulse, breathing and, with an Apple Watch, coherence. It does not use the formulas on this page.

sections.highlight: Positive means beats were spreading out (pulse slowing); negative means they were bunching up (pulse rising).

slope.title: HR Trend Slope: Is Your Pulse Rising or Falling?
slope.seoTitle: HR Trend Slope: Is Your Pulse Rising or Falling?

sections.heading: What this number shows
sections.body: The HR trend slope tells you whether your heart rate was drifting up or down across the current measurement window. It is useful for watching a change happen in real time, such as your pulse settling as you breathe slowly or climbing after you stand up.

sections.heading: How this tool calculates it
sections.body: The tool fits a straight line (linear regression) through your RR intervals in order, beat by beat. It then flips the sign and divides by 100, so that a positive value means heart rate is rising (intervals getting shorter) and a negative value means heart rate is falling (intervals getting longer). The tool works on a rolling 15-second window of fingertip video (about 30 frames per second), finds each pulse peak, keeps only beat-to-beat (RR) intervals between 400 and 1,500 ms that are within 22% of the median, and smooths the displayed numbers so they change gradually.

bullets.label: Positive
bullets.text: Your pulse was trending upward during the window: for example after moving, talking, standing, or during tension.

bullets.label: Negative
bullets.text: Your pulse was trending downward: common when you sit down, relax, or breathe slowly with longer exhales.

bullets.label: Close to zero
bullets.text: Heart rate was roughly flat. At steady rest this is what you would expect.

sections.heading: Why it can be noisy
sections.body: Within 15 seconds your heart rate naturally rises and falls with each breath, so the fitted line can tilt one way or the other just because of where the window starts. Camera-based beat timing also has small errors. Look for a consistent sign over half a minute or more rather than reacting to a single value.

sections.heading: A simple experiment
sections.body: Sit still, let the reading settle, then breathe slowly: about 4 seconds in and 6 seconds out for a minute. Many people see the slope move toward negative values as their pulse eases down. Then stand up and watch it turn positive as heart rate briefly rises.

sections.heading: Important limits
sections.body: This is a real-time trend indicator for this browser tool. It has no standard normal range and is not a medical measurement.
The ONDA app is a separate product: it focuses on pulse, breathing and, with an Apple Watch, coherence. It does not use the formulas on this page.

sections.highlight: Positive means your pulse is climbing; negative means it is easing down.

recovery.title: Recovery Rate: How Fast Your Pulse Settles
recovery.seoTitle: Recovery Rate: How Fast Your Pulse Settles

sections.heading: What this number shows
sections.body: Recovery Rate in this tool is a within-window measure. It looks at the highest heart rate in the last 15 seconds and asks how far the most recent beat has come back from that peak toward the window average. It is not the same as the clinical "heart rate recovery" test, which measures how many beats per minute your pulse drops in the first minute after hard exercise.

sections.heading: How this tool calculates it
sections.body: For each beat the tool converts the RR interval to beats per minute. If the peak is at least 2 bpm above the window average, Recovery = (peak − latest beat) ÷ (peak − average) × 100, limited to 0–100%. If there was no clear peak, the value is 0. The tool works on a rolling 15-second window of fingertip video (about 30 frames per second), finds each pulse peak, keeps only beat-to-beat (RR) intervals between 400 and 1,500 ms that are within 22% of the median, and smooths the displayed numbers so they change gradually.

bullets.label: Near 100%
bullets.text: The latest beat is back at (or below) your average for the window, so any short spike has passed.

bullets.label: Around 50%
bullets.text: Your pulse is about halfway back from its recent peak.

bullets.label: Near 0%
bullets.text: Either your pulse is still at its peak, or there was no noticeable peak at all (a steady reading also shows 0). Check the other numbers to tell these apart.

sections.heading: Why it moves a lot
sections.body: Heart rate naturally rises on each inhale and falls on each exhale, so the "peak" is often just the top of a breath cycle and the value can swing from beat to beat. A single false or missed beat from the camera can also create an artificial peak.

sections.heading: Recovery in the broader sense
sections.body: Over hours and days, recovery is better judged by trends: morning resting heart rate, HRV measured the same way each day, sleep, and how you feel. After exercise, a faster drop in heart rate during the first minute is generally a sign of good fitness.

sections.heading: Important limits
sections.body: This is a rough, experimental indicator of this browser tool, not a medical or training metric.
The ONDA app is a separate product: it focuses on pulse, breathing and, with an Apple Watch, coherence. It does not use the formulas on this page.

sections.highlight: High means your pulse is back near its average after a recent peak; 0% can also simply mean there was no peak.

sections.heading: What this number shows
sections.body: CSI in this tool is the coefficient of variation of your beat-to-beat intervals: how much the intervals vary compared with their average length. Because it is divided by the mean interval, it lets you compare rhythm evenness at different heart rates. Lower means the intervals were more alike; higher means more variation.

sections.heading: How this tool calculates it
sections.body: CSI = standard deviation of the RR intervals ÷ mean RR interval. For example, if your intervals average 800 ms with a standard deviation of 40 ms, CSI is 0.05. The tool works on a rolling 15-second window of fingertip video (about 30 frames per second), finds each pulse peak, keeps only beat-to-beat (RR) intervals between 400 and 1,500 ms that are within 22% of the median, and smooths the displayed numbers so they change gradually.

sections.heading: Why camera values look high
sections.body: With a phone camera, beat timing is only accurate to a few milliseconds and some peaks are misplaced, so the measured spread is larger than the true one. In practice readings around 0.3 are typical on this page; lower values mean a cleaner, steadier signal.

bullets.label: Lower (well under 0.3)
bullets.text: Intervals were fairly even and the signal was clean.

bullets.label: Around 0.3
bullets.text: A typical camera reading.

bullets.label: Clearly higher
bullets.text: Intervals varied a lot: often movement, pressing too hard, cold fingers or poor light; occasionally genuinely irregular beats.

sections.heading: CSI and heart rate variability
sections.body: Some variation between beats is healthy: the heart speeds up slightly on each inhale and slows on each exhale, and people with good fitness often show more of this at rest. So lower is not automatically "better" in physiology. In this tool, however, CSI is mainly a check on how steady and clean the reading was, and it feeds the Stress (130 × CSI), Energy, Relaxation and Alarm indices.

sections.heading: Health note
sections.body: If you notice a persistently irregular pulse, palpitations, dizziness or shortness of breath, see a doctor. A browser camera reading cannot detect or rule out arrhythmias such as atrial fibrillation.
The ONDA app is a separate product: it focuses on pulse, breathing and, with an Apple Watch, coherence. It does not use the formulas on this page.

sections.highlight: CSI is the spread of your beat intervals divided by their average; typical camera readings sit around 0.3.

sections.heading: What HRV is
sections.body: Heart rate variability (HRV) is the natural variation in time between heartbeats. A healthy heart does not tick like a metronome: intervals lengthen and shorten with breathing, posture and nervous-system activity. RMSSD, the root mean square of successive differences, is one of the most widely used HRV measures and mainly reflects parasympathetic (vagal) activity, the "rest and digest" side of the nervous system.

sections.heading: How this tool calculates it
sections.body: The tool takes each pair of consecutive RR intervals, squares their difference, averages those squares and takes the square root, giving a value in milliseconds. Values above 100 ms are capped at 100. The tool works on a rolling 15-second window of fingertip video (about 30 frames per second), finds each pulse peak, keeps only beat-to-beat (RR) intervals between 400 and 1,500 ms that are within 22% of the median, and smooths the displayed numbers so they change gradually.

sections.heading: Typical ranges and what affects them
sections.body: For short daytime readings like this one, resting RMSSD in healthy adults varies widely, often roughly 20–80 ms. Age and time of day matter: it tends to be higher in younger and fitter people, lower with age, and night-time values from a watch are usually higher than daytime spot checks. See [normal HRV by age](/articles/normal-hrv-by-age) or try the [HRV tool](/tools/hrv). It usually drops after poor sleep, alcohol, illness, intense training or acute stress, and rises with good recovery. Differences between people are large, so your own trend matters more than comparison with others.

bullets.label: Higher than your usual
bullets.text: Often seen when rested and relaxed.

bullets.label: Lower than your usual
bullets.text: Common with fatigue, stress, alcohol, illness or a late heavy meal.

sections.heading: Why camera readings are rough
sections.body: RMSSD depends on millisecond-level timing. A phone camera at about 30 frames per second, a fingertip that shifts slightly, and a window of only 15 seconds all add error, usually inflating the value. Standard short-term HRV measurements use at least a few minutes of ECG or a chest strap. Treat the number here as a rough estimate and compare readings only when taken the same way.

bullets.label: Measure consistently
bullets.text: For trends, measure at the same time (for example after waking), sitting still, breathing normally.

bullets.label: Slow breathing
bullets.text: Slow breathing at around 6 breaths per minute typically increases beat-to-beat variation while you do it.

bullets.label: Basics first
bullets.text: Regular sleep, limited alcohol and aerobic exercise are associated with higher resting HRV over time.

sections.body: The ONDA app is a separate product: it focuses on pulse, breathing and, with an Apple Watch, coherence. It does not use the formulas on this page.

sections.highlight: RMSSD reflects vagal activity; the camera version here is a rough estimate, most useful when compared with your own readings.

sections.heading: What this number is
sections.body: Energy here is an experimental index, not a measure of how energetic you feel, your fitness, or a "battery". It starts at 90% and goes down when your heart rate is above 75 bpm and when your beat-to-beat rhythm is irregular relative to its average (CSI).

sections.heading: How this tool calculates it
sections.body: Energy = 90 − 1.5 × (heart rate − 75, if above 75) − 80 × CSI, limited to 10–100%. For example, at 70 bpm with a typical camera CSI of 0.3, Energy is about 66%; at 95 bpm with the same CSI, it is about 36%. The tool works on a rolling 15-second window of fingertip video (about 30 frames per second), finds each pulse peak, keeps only beat-to-beat (RR) intervals between 400 and 1,500 ms that are within 22% of the median, and smooths the displayed numbers so they change gradually.

bullets.label: Higher
bullets.text: Your pulse was at or below about 75 bpm and the rhythm looked steady.

bullets.label: Lower
bullets.text: A faster pulse (coffee, movement, heat, stress, illness) and/or an irregular-looking rhythm, which is often just a noisy signal.

sections.heading: Important limits
sections.body: This is an experimental heuristic built from a few camera-derived inputs. It is not a validated physiological measure, it is not emotion detection, and it is not a medical test. Treat it as a rough hint about the direction your signal is moving, not as a verdict about how you feel. Because of the formula, Energy cannot exceed 90% and a resting pulse below 75 bpm is not rewarded any further.

bullets.label: Sleep
bullets.text: Consistent, sufficient sleep is the strongest lever for daytime energy.

bullets.label: Movement and daylight
bullets.text: A short walk, especially outdoors in the morning, often helps more than extra caffeine.

bullets.label: Short resets
bullets.text: A few minutes of slow breathing can lower a racing pulse and help you feel more settled.

sections.body: The ONDA app is a separate product: it focuses on pulse, breathing and, with an Apple Watch, coherence. It does not use the formulas on this page.

sections.highlight: Energy here drops with a pulse above 75 bpm and an irregular-looking rhythm. It is a rough hint, not a fuel gauge.

sections.heading: What this number is
sections.body: Stress on this page is an experimental index. It is simply the Cardiac Stability Index (CSI), the variation of your beat-to-beat intervals relative to their average, rescaled to a percentage. It does not measure stress hormones, emotions or how stressed you feel, and it is not a validated stress score.

sections.heading: How this tool calculates it
sections.body: Stress = 130 × CSI, limited to 0–100%. A typical camera CSI of about 0.3 gives roughly 40%. Heart rate and breathing rate are not part of this formula. The tool works on a rolling 15-second window of fingertip video (about 30 frames per second), finds each pulse peak, keeps only beat-to-beat (RR) intervals between 400 and 1,500 ms that are within 22% of the median, and smooths the displayed numbers so they change gradually.

bullets.label: Higher
bullets.text: Your beat intervals varied more relative to their mean. That can accompany tension, but the most common cause on a phone camera is signal noise: moving your finger, pressing too hard, cold hands or weak light.

bullets.label: Lower
bullets.text: The intervals were more even and the signal was cleaner.

sections.heading: Important limits
sections.body: This is an experimental heuristic built from a few camera-derived inputs. It is not a validated physiological measure, it is not emotion detection, and it is not a medical test. Treat it as a rough hint about the direction your signal is moving, not as a verdict about how you feel. In real physiology, acute stress usually lowers short-term heart rate variability rather than raising it, so a higher irregularity score is not a reliable stress sign. If stress is affecting your daily life, talking to a professional is more useful than any reading.

bullets.label: Slow breathing with a longer exhale
bullets.text: Several minutes of slow breathing is one of the simplest ways to calm the body.

bullets.label: Better readings
bullets.text: Rest your forearm on a table, cover the camera lightly and hold still for 30 seconds or more before looking at the number.

bullets.label: Daily habits
bullets.text: Sleep, regular exercise, time outdoors and social contact all help with long-term stress.

sections.highlight: Stress here is 130 × CSI: a rough rhythm-irregularity hint, strongly affected by signal quality.

br.title: Breathing Rate: Breaths per Minute Explained
br.seoTitle: Breathing Rate: Breaths per Minute Explained

sections.heading: What breathing rate is
sections.body: Breathing (respiratory) rate is the number of breaths you take per minute. It is one of the basic vital signs, and it is also the one you can change most easily on purpose, which is why slow breathing is used in many relaxation methods.

sections.heading: How this tool calculates it
sections.body: Breathing slightly changes the strength of each pulse wave in your fingertip. The tool smooths the size of the pulse signal over about 5 seconds, finds the peaks of that slow wave (at least 2 seconds apart), takes the median time between them and converts it to breaths per minute. It shows a value only when it finds at least five such peaks and the result is between 6 and 30 breaths per minute; otherwise it shows nothing. Because the window is short and the effect is subtle, this is an approximate estimate.

bullets.label: About 12–20 per minute
bullets.text: The usual resting range for adults.

bullets.label: Slower (about 6–10)
bullets.text: Common during deliberate slow breathing, meditation or deep rest.

bullets.label: Faster (above about 20 at rest)
bullets.text: Can come with exertion, anxiety, fever or illness. Persistently fast breathing at rest, or breathlessness, is worth checking with a doctor.

sections.heading: Why slow breathing is popular
sections.body: Breathing slowly, often around 5.5–6 breaths per minute (individually about 4.5–7) with a relaxed, longer exhale, tends to increase the heart-rate swings that follow each breath and is associated with feeling calmer. It is a low-risk, well-studied technique. If you feel lightheaded, return to normal breathing.

sections.heading: Tips for a better reading
sections.body: Rest your hand, keep the finger still with light pressure, breathe naturally, and give the tool at least 20–30 seconds. Talking or moving makes the estimate unreliable.
The ONDA app is a separate product: it focuses on pulse, breathing and, with an Apple Watch, coherence. It does not use the formulas on this page.

sections.highlight: Breathing rate here is estimated from the slow rise and fall of your pulse signal; treat it as approximate.

bpm.title: BPM: Your Heart Rate and What Changes It
bpm.seoTitle: BPM: Your Heart Rate and What Changes It

sections.heading: What heart rate is
sections.body: Heart rate is the number of heartbeats per minute (bpm). It rises when your body needs more blood flow, for example during movement, heat, stress, illness or after caffeine, and falls during rest and sleep. Resting heart rate is a useful everyday health marker when you track it over time.

sections.heading: How this tool calculates it
sections.body: Your fingertip over the camera changes color slightly with each pulse (photoplethysmography, PPG). The tool finds each pulse peak in the red channel, measures the time between peaks (RR intervals), drops implausible ones, and computes heart rate as 60,000 divided by the average interval in milliseconds. Results outside 40–180 bpm are discarded. The tool works on a rolling 15-second window of fingertip video (about 30 frames per second), finds each pulse peak, keeps only beat-to-beat (RR) intervals between 400 and 1,500 ms that are within 22% of the median, and smooths the displayed numbers so they change gradually.

bullets.label: About 60–100 bpm
bullets.text: The commonly cited normal resting range for adults. Many healthy people, especially active ones, rest lower.

bullets.label: Below 60 bpm
bullets.text: Often normal in fit people and during deep rest; see a doctor if it comes with dizziness, fainting or unusual tiredness.

bullets.label: Above 100 bpm at rest
bullets.text: Can follow caffeine, stress, dehydration or illness. If it stays high at rest or comes with chest pain or breathlessness, seek medical advice.

sections.heading: How accurate is a camera reading?
sections.body: Camera heart rate is usually close to a reference device when you hold still in good light, but it is less reliable with movement, cold fingers, heavy pressure or dim lighting. It is an educational estimate, not a medical measurement.

bullets.label: Measure resting HR consistently
bullets.text: For example sitting quietly for a minute after waking, before coffee.

bullets.label: Slow breathing
bullets.text: A few minutes of slow breathing with a longer exhale often lowers heart rate a little.

bullets.label: Long-term habits
bullets.text: Regular aerobic exercise, good sleep and limited alcohol tend to lower resting heart rate over weeks.

sections.highlight: Heart rate is easiest to learn from when you measure it the same way each time and look at the trend.
